name: Northern Taiwan Wealth-Praying Day Trip
transport: All by MRT and on foot — no car needed. An EasyCard covers every train and bus.
summary: Three of Taipei's busiest wealth-praying temples in a single day. Start the morning at Xingtian Temple, where Guan Sheng Dijun — Lord Guan, the merchants' patron of loyalty and good faith — presides over the 'honest wealth' earned by fair dealing. Around midday, cross town to Songshan Ciyou Temple, where Mazu is asked for the quieter blessing of a safe, steady livelihood. By late afternoon you reach the Xia-Hai City God Temple on Dihua Street, where the City God governs opportunity and fortune — and Yue Lao, the Matchmaker God, waits in the same small hall. Finish at Dadaocheng Wharf as the sun goes down over the river. Every stop is a short walk from an MRT station.

stops.prayFor: A thriving career and honest wealth
stops.why: Xingtian Temple is dedicated to Guan Sheng Dijun — Lord Guan (Guan Yu) — whom the business world treats as its guardian. His two great virtues, loyalty and keeping one's word, are exactly the 'honest wealth' that merchants come to pray for. It is one of the busiest temples in Taipei, and its free soul-calming (shoujing) blessing is a quiet ritual worth witnessing.
stops.tips: Xingtian Temple burns no incense, sells no gold paper, and keeps no donation box — you simply press your palms together and pray. The soul-calming line can get long, so a weekday morning is your best bet.
stops.arrival: MRT Xingtian Temple Station, Exit 3 — about a 3-minute walk

stops.prayFor: Peaceful prosperity and a settled household
stops.why: Songshan Ciyou Temple is the spiritual heart of the Songshan district, dedicated to Mazu, the Heavenly Holy Mother. Beyond wealth, what Mazu grants is 'prospering in peace' — settle yourself first, then let the business grow. It is the old merchants' wisdom.
stops.tips: The temple sits right at the mouth of the Raohe Street Night Market. If your day runs into the evening, praying and then wandering straight into the market is the local move.
stops.arrival: MRT Songshan Station, Exit 5 — about a 2-minute walk

stops.prayFor: Opportune fortune, good connections, and love
stops.why: The Xia-Hai City God Temple on Dihua Street is famous across Taiwan for its Yue Lao, the Matchmaker God — but the City God himself governs a district's rewards, punishments, and chances. For a person in business, this is where you pray for the 'fortune of timing': the right moment, the right people, the right connections.
stops.tips: The temple is small, but the stream of worshippers never stops. Afterward, walk the length of Dihua Street — the dried-goods sellers, herbal-medicine halls, and fabric shops are century-old family businesses, and it is the most characterful place to pick up a gift to take home.
stops.arrival: MRT Beimen Station, Exit 3 — about a 10-minute walk; or a 12-minute walk from Daqiaotou Station

itinerary.activity: Xingtian Temple (Guan Sheng Dijun — praying for career and honest wealth)
MRT from Xingtian Temple Station to Songshan Station (change at Zhongshan Junior High for the Songshan line, about 20 minutes)
Songshan Ciyou Temple (Mazu — praying for peaceful prosperity)
Lunch around Raohe Street: Fuzhou pepper buns and herbal pork-rib soup
MRT from Songshan Station to Beimen Station (about 25 minutes)
Xia-Hai City God Temple (City God & Yue Lao — praying for opportunity)
Stroll Dihua Street: dried goods and gifts to take home
Finish at Dadaocheng Wharf for the sunset over the Tamsui River

notes: All three temples are free to enter. Crowds swell on the 1st and 15th of the lunar month and on weekends, so if you prefer some quiet, go on a weekday. The general rule for wealth-praying: state your name, birth date, and address, explain what you are asking for, and pledge only a thanks-offering you can comfortably keep.

food.name: Raohe St. Night Market — Fuzhou Pepper Buns
food.description: Songshan Ciyou Temple sits right at the entrance to Raohe Street Night Market, and slipping straight in after praying to Mazu is the local move. The name to know here is the Fuzhou pepper bun — slapped onto the wall of a charcoal oven and baked fresh, the crust comes out blistered and crisp, and the first bite floods with peppery pork and scallion. Worth the wait in line.

food.name: Dadaocheng — Dried Goods & Traditional Pastries
food.description: Dihua Street, home to the Xia-Hai City God Temple, has been Taipei's dried-goods heart for over a century. Once you've prayed to the City God and Yue Lao, work your way down the street: the herbal-medicine halls, dried-goods sellers, and old pastry shops are the place to pick up a gift. A box of traditional Chinese pastries or a bag of dried goods carries far more of Dadaocheng than any night-market snack.

name: Taipei Classic Temple Half-Day Tour
transport: Entirely by MRT + walking. Grab an EasyCard at any station — it works on all trains and buses.
summary: Visiting Taipei for the first time and want to see its temples? This is the route. Start your morning at Longshan Temple, the city's most celebrated temple with nearly 300 years of incense smoke and some of Taiwan's finest carving craftsmanship. In the afternoon, head to the Xia-Hai City God Temple on Dihua Street — its Matchmaker God (Yue Lao) is so famous that travelers fly in from Japan and Korea just to pray for love. End the day strolling Dadaocheng's heritage street with a coffee and some local goods. Both temples are free to enter, and everything is reachable by MRT.

stops.prayFor: Safety, health, and love — Guanyin and the Matchmaker God are both here
stops.why: Founded in 1738, Manka Longshan Temple is Taipei's oldest and most internationally renowned temple. Its stone pillars, woodwork, and jiannian mosaic roof are considered the pinnacle of Taiwanese temple artistry. The main hall honors Guanyin (the Bodhisattva of Compassion), while the rear hall houses Yue Lao, the Matchmaker God — Buddhist and Taoist deities under one roof, which is exactly how folk religion works in Taiwan.
stops.tips: First time at a Taiwanese temple? Read our Temple Visiting Guide first: enter through the Dragon Gate (right side), exit through the Tiger Gate (left side), and always step OVER the threshold, never on it. Photos are fine inside, but skip the flash and avoid pointing your camera at people who are praying.
stops.arrival: MRT Longshan Temple Station, Exit 1 — about a 2-minute walk

stops.prayFor: Love and marriage (Taiwan's most famous Matchmaker), plus career luck
stops.why: The Xia-Hai City God Temple on Dihua Street is tiny — under 165 square meters — yet it is Taiwan's most famous temple for praying for love. Its Yue Lao is credited with thousands of successful matches every year and has been featured repeatedly in Japanese media. The temple provides prayer instructions in English, Japanese, and Chinese, so you can follow along even without knowing a word of Mandarin.
stops.tips: Praying to Yue Lao has its own ritual (the temple has an illustrated guide): purchase the offering set with the red thread, introduce yourself to Yue Lao and describe the partner you hope to meet, then keep the red thread with you. Already have a partner? Thank Yue Lao and pray for a lasting relationship instead.
stops.arrival: MRT Beimen Station, Exit 3 — about a 10-minute walk

itinerary.activity: Longshan Temple (Guanyin & Yue Lao)
Stroll Bopiliao Historic Block next door — preserved Qing-dynasty street houses
Lunch around Huaxi Street: pepper buns, squid thick soup, and other local snacks
MRT from Longshan Temple Station to Beimen Station (about 15 minutes)
Xia-Hai City God Temple (City God & Yue Lao)
Dihua Street: dried goods shops, Chinese medicine halls, indie stores and heritage-house cafés
Finish at Dadaocheng Wharf with a view over the Tamsui River

notes: Both temples are free to enter with no reservation needed. There is no strict dress code, but avoid overly revealing clothing out of respect. Incense and offerings can be purchased at the temples (Longshan Temple has phased out incense burning — praying with palms together is the norm there). For the full etiquette walkthrough, see our Temple Visiting Guide.

food.name: Manka — Huaxi Street Old-Taipei Eats
food.description: Step out of Longshan Temple and you're in the oldest quarter of Manka, right beside Huaxi Street Night Market. This stretch is old Taipei in miniature — sesame-oil pork kidney, oyster vermicelli, old-fashioned sweet soups, much of it from shops that have kept the same flavors for decades. A bowl here after the temple is a taste of a century of Wanhua street life.

food.name: Dadaocheng — Cisheng Temple Courtyard Food Street
food.description: Over in Dadaocheng, beyond the dried-goods shops of Dihua Street, those in the know turn into the food street in front of Cisheng Temple. Tables and chairs are set out in a long row under an old banyan tree — fried snacks, fish soup, pork-rib soup with a bowl of rice. It is one of the few places left in Taipei where you can eat quietly in a temple courtyard's shade, and it suits a solo traveler well.

name: Dajia Mazu Pilgrimage Trail
transport: Driving is easiest (Dajia to Xingang is about 1.5 hours on the freeway). Rail plus a connecting bus works too, but the transfers eat time — for one person, driving is the most unhurried way to go.
summary: Every year in the third lunar month, millions join the palanquin of the Dajia Mazu for a nine-day, eight-night walk of more than 300 kilometers — but this route asks you to skip those nine days, and to walk only the first and last stops. Pick a weekday, and go alone: at dawn, Dajia Zhenlan Temple holds nothing but the footsteps of locals lighting their morning incense; in the afternoon, Xingang Fengtian Temple lets you linger over Ye Wang's cochin pottery, then sit on a bench in the temple courtyard until you no longer want to leave. The 300 kilometers in between belong to the millions who walk them with Mazu each year; you don't need the whole road. At the two ends, say what is on your mind plainly — and that is your pilgrimage.

stops.prayFor: A safe setting-out, and telling Mazu what is on your mind
stops.why: Dajia Zhenlan Temple is the most famous Mazu temple in Taiwan and the starting point of the nine-day, eight-night pilgrimage. During the procession it is shoulder to shoulder here — but on an ordinary weekday morning, the hall usually holds only locals going about their daily worship: the same Mazu, an entirely different quiet. The 276-kilogram solid-gold Mazu statue downstairs is yours to see, too, without the crush of a crowd.
stops.tips: Weekday mornings are the calmest; the 1st and 15th of the lunar month and weekends are noticeably busier. Tell Mazu that today you are walking a pilgrimage of your own, alone — then don't rush off. Sit in the courtyard a while first. For a gift to take home, Dajia's famous crumbly butter shortcakes come from the old house Yu Zhen Xin, which has shops right around the temple.
stops.arrival: About a 10-minute walk from Dajia Rail Station; by car, exit National Freeway 3 at the Dajia interchange

stops.prayFor: A vow fulfilled, and the Tiger General's guard over your wealth
stops.why: Xingang Fengtian Temple is known as the home of the 'First Mazu in Taiwan' and is the end point of the Dajia Mazu pilgrimage each year — stand here and you have walked, alone, both the head and the tail of the whole route. Its Tiger General (Huye) is enshrined on top of the altar table rather than beneath it as is usual, and the old saying 'the herald of Beigang, the Tiger General of Xingang' speaks to his renown. The temple's treasures are the cochin-pottery works of the master Ye Wang.
stops.tips: Weekday afternoons draw few pilgrims — take your time finding Ye Wang's cochin pottery, no need to hurry. The duck-meat thick soup by the temple gate is a taste locals have known since childhood: a seat to sit down in, and no line. Buy a pack of Xingang taffy, carry it to a bench in the courtyard, and eat it with the sunset — that bench is where this route ends.
stops.arrival: From Chiayi Rail Station, take a Beigang-bound bus and get off at the Xingang Fengtian Temple stop, about 40 minutes; by car, exit National Freeway 1 at Dalin or Minxiong and follow the county road

itinerary.activity: Dajia Zhenlan Temple (Mazu — telling her you are setting out on a pilgrimage of your own) — quietest at dawn on a weekday
Sit in the courtyard a while; pick up a box of butter shortcakes on Shuntian Road, unhurried
Drive south to Xingang (about 1.5 hours on the freeway) — nothing scheduled along the way
Lunch by the Xingang temple gate: a bowl of duck-meat thick soup, eaten slowly, sitting down
Xingang Fengtian Temple (First Mazu, the Tiger General & Ye Wang's cochin pottery)
Sit on a courtyard bench with Xingang taffy and the sunset — this is the end; no rush home

notes: Both temples are free to enter. The point of this route is to walk Mazu's road while avoiding the crowds: during the Dajia Mazu procession (the setting-out date is chosen by divination blocks, usually around the third lunar month) the whole route is packed, so steer clear of those nine days; the 1st and 15th of the lunar month and weekends are noticeably busier too, and a weekday-morning start is ideal. Reporting in alone is simple: your name and why you have come, said to Mazu — that is all. If you still have time on the way back, Changhua Nanyao Temple (the first-night resting place of the Dajia procession, whose rear Guanyin hall has rare Greek-style column capitals), just off the Changhua interchange, is worth a look — but that is a bonus, not homework.

food.name: Dajia — Butter Shortcake & Taro Cake
food.description: The old street outside Dajia Zhenlan Temple is best known for its butter shortcake — Dajia's signature specialty, with a crust that flakes apart in crisp layers around a sweet malt-and-butter filling. It's good warm or cool, and one of Taichung's most classic gifts to bring home. Dajia is also taro country, so the taro cake is every bit as local a treat.

food.name: Xingang — Xingang Taffy & Duck Thick Soup
food.description: Xingang, the trail's final stop and home to Fengtian Temple, is famous above all for Xingang taffy — a traditional sweet made from malt sugar and peanuts, soft with a gentle chew, and made here for over a century. Around the temple gate, the duck thick soup and sweet-potato noodles are old flavors locals have known since childhood.

name: Tainan Old-Capital Temple Walk
transport: All on foot — the three stops are all in Tainan's West Central District, never more than a 10-minute walk apart. Just right for one person.
summary: By mid-morning on a weekday, the incense smoke at the Grand Mazu Temple outnumbers the visitors — this is the best hour to see the old capital of Tainan. This route is built for walking alone, and it has only three stops: the Tainan Grand Mazu Temple, Taiwan's first official Mazu temple (and once the palace of the Ming loyalist Prince Ningjing); the Grand Martial Temple one lane over, with its 66-meter vermilion wall; and, a few minutes' walk on, the Tainan Tiantan, the Altar of Heaven. The three sit less than ten minutes apart on foot, and you can walk them in a single afternoon with time to spare — the benches in the temple courtyards, a bowl of unhurried fish soup down a side lane, a plate of sliced fruit at the old Lily Fruit Shop across from the Confucius Temple: that is the real body of this walk. Three-hundred-year-old Tainan isn't going anywhere. Take it slow — that is exactly enough.

stops.prayFor: Peace, and warmth in love (its Yue Lao watches over the one-sided and the deepening)
stops.why: The Tainan Grand Mazu Temple is the only Mazu temple in Taiwan built by imperial decree, and once the palace of the Ming loyalist Prince Ningjing, Zhu Shugui — the only temple in Taiwan converted from a prince's residence. The Yue Lao in the rear hall is said to look after those in unrequited love and those praying for a relationship to grow warmer; come alone, and you have all the time you need to say it out loud.
stops.tips: Weekday mornings draw the fewest worshippers — the hall is quiet enough to hear your own footsteps. The Grand Mazu Temple hides down a lane off Yongfu Road: an unassuming front, a world within. The Qing imperial plaque 'Huihuang Haishi' hangs inside the hall — look up and find it.
stops.arrival: About a 20-minute walk from Tainan Rail Station; or take a city bus to the 'Chihkan Tower' stop, then walk about 3 minutes

stops.prayFor: Uprightness in your work, and cutting off bad romantic luck
stops.why: The Grand Martial Temple is the only Guan Di temple in Taiwan included in the official state rites, right next door to the Grand Mazu Temple. Its 66-meter vermilion wall, rising and falling along the lane and praised as the 'finest in Jiangnan,' is worth walking slowly beneath more than photographing. Inside hangs the plaque 'Da Zhang Fu' (A True Man) in the hand of the Qing Yongzheng Emperor, and the statue of Guan Sheng Dijun, eyes blazing, radiates the martial saint's upright force.
stops.tips: The Yifeng winter-melon tea stand directly across from the temple gate keeps a permanent line — a glance at the queue as you pass is plenty; no need to join it, when the side lanes are full of old shops where you can actually sit down. The red wall catches the light in the afternoon, so if you want a photo, loop back to it before you leave.
stops.arrival: About a 1-minute walk from the Grand Mazu Temple — the two are neighbors

stops.prayFor: Life's big turning points — the one wish that matters most (the Jade Emperor is highest of all)
stops.why: The Tainan Tiantan, commonly called the 'Heaven God Temple,' is Taiwan's first altar dedicated solely to the Jade Emperor, where Qing officials made their annual offerings to Heaven. The single-character plaque 'Yi' (One) high in the main hall is called the most valuable plaque in all Taiwan — because the Jade Emperor is supreme, and of a thousand words only the one character 'One' can stand for it.
stops.tips: Tainan people come to pray to the Jade Emperor only for the big things: a move, a new business, an exam, a marriage. If there is one wish on this trip that matters most to you, save it for this stop. For quiet, avoid the ninth day of the first lunar month (the Jade Emperor's birthday) and the 1st and 15th — a weekday afternoon is the most serene.
stops.arrival: About a 5-minute walk from the Grand Martial Temple

itinerary.activity: Tainan Grand Mazu Temple (Mazu & Yue Lao) — fewest worshippers on a weekday morning
Grand Martial Temple (Guan Sheng Dijun); walk the vermilion wall slowly; passing the Yifeng winter-melon tea, one glance at the line is enough
Lunch: duck down a side lane for a noodle or fish-soup shop with seats — the kind with no queue and an owner who won't rush you — and eat slowly
Tainan Tiantan (Jade Emperor & the 'Yi' plaque); save your most important wish for the Jade Emperor, then sit a while in the courtyard
Walk about 10 minutes south to the Lily Fruit Shop across from the Confucius Temple to wind down — an old shop with seats, a plate of sliced fruit, and stay as long as you like

notes: All three stops are free to enter. For quiet, come on a weekday and avoid the 1st and 15th of the lunar month and weekends; the ninth day of the first lunar month, the Jade Emperor's birthday, is the Tiantan's grandest and most crowded day. Walking alone, there is no schedule to keep — the lanes between the temples are the scenery themselves, so if you lose your way, don't rush to check the map. If you still have energy, Chihkan Tower (the base of the fort the Dutch built in 1653; ticketed), on the block directly across from the Grand Martial Temple, is quietest after its evening lights come on — a worthy add-on; if you are spent, save it for next time.

food.name: Old Capital — Dawn Tainan Beef Soup
food.description: In Tainan the day often begins with a bowl of beef soup. Freshly sliced same-day beef is cooked the instant a scalding broth is poured over it, so the meat stays pink and tender. If you set out early on this walk, find a bowl of beef soup with a side of minced-pork rice around Chihkan Tower for breakfast — it's the most authentic Tainan morning ritual there is.

food.name: Around Chihkan Tower — Traditional Old-Capital Snacks
food.description: The Grand Mazu Temple and Grand Martial Temple sit right beside Chihkan Tower, in the densest cluster of Tainan street food anywhere in the old city. Savory rice pudding, danzai noodles, shrimp rolls, coffin bread, thin noodles — these are flavors the old capital has passed down for decades, and you'll cross one stall after another every few steps. The point here isn't to keep a schedule; it's to wander slowly and eat whatever you happen upon.

name: Tainan Yue Lao Love-Praying Escape
transport: All on foot — the two temples stand side by side on Yongfu Road. Just right for a slow walk on your own.
summary: When love feels stuck, plenty of Tainan folk quietly take a walk down Yongfu Road, alone. This route has just two stops, both in Tainan's West Central District and next door to each other: first the Grand Martial Temple, to ask its Yue Lao — the Matchmaker God — to sever the bad romances and troublemakers still tangling up your past; then a one-minute walk to the Grand Mazu Temple, to pray to Tainan's most trusted Yue Lao for a good match. Each of Tainan's Four Great Yue Lao has its own calling, and this route follows the most natural pairing of the four: clear out the old first, then make your wish. Half a day to walk it, and the empty space is left for you.

stops.prayFor: Cutting off bad romance, ending toxic ties, and warding off troublemakers
stops.why: The Grand Martial Temple is dedicated to Guan Sheng Dijun — Lord Guan — and the Yue Lao beside him is the most unusual of Tainan's Four Great Yue Lao: he specializes in cutting off bad romance and warding off the troublemakers in your life. A past you can't let go of, an entanglement you can't cut, a third party or a toxic person clinging on — this is where you come first, to ask Yue Lao to cut the knot with a single clean stroke. Clear away the bad ties first, so the good ones have room to come in.
stops.tips: To pray to Yue Lao, bring a red thread and offerings (wedding candy, fresh flowers); the temple usually provides gold paper and instructions. Cutting off bad romance has its own ritual and its own order of things to say — if you're unsure, ask a temple volunteer, they're glad to show you. For quiet, pick a weekday morning.
stops.arrival: About a 20-minute walk from Tainan Rail Station; or take a city bus to the 'Chihkan Tower' stop, then walk about 3 minutes

stops.prayFor: A good match, a one-sided love returned, and a warming relationship
stops.why: The Tainan Grand Mazu Temple is Taiwan's first official Mazu temple, and the Yue Lao in its rear hall is the foremost of Tainan's Four Great Yue Lao — his reputation for answered prayers is known to everyone in the old capital. He looks after those in unrequited love and blesses steady relationships to keep growing warmer. The last stop cleared out the bad romance; here you hand him your wish — for the right match, one that lasts.
stops.tips: Before Yue Lao, sincerely report your name, your birth date, and the match you hope for — the more specific, the better. Carry the red thread you receive with you. The two temples are only a minute apart, yet the mood is completely different: the Martial Temple is imposing, the Grand Mazu Temple warm and gentle. Take your time to feel it.
stops.arrival: About a 1-minute walk from the Grand Martial Temple — the two are neighbors

itinerary.activity: Grand Martial Temple (Yue Lao — cutting off bad romance and warding off troublemakers)
About a 1-minute walk to the Grand Mazu Temple
Grand Mazu Temple (Yue Lao — praying for a good match and a warming relationship)
Lunch around Yongfu Road, and a slow wander

notes: Both stops are free to enter. For quiet, pick a weekday morning and avoid the 1st and 15th of the lunar month and weekends. There's no rush when you're praying for love — walking this route alone is meant to be a quiet stretch of time to sort out your own heart, so it's fine to go slow. Tainan's other two Great Yue Lao are at Chongqing Temple (for winning a love back) and Daguanyin Pavilion (for finding a match); if you still have the energy and the heart to walk further that day, extend the route yourself — if you're spent, save it for next time.

food.name: Old Capital — Dawn Tainan Beef Soup
food.description: In Tainan the day often begins with a bowl of beef soup. Freshly sliced same-day beef cooks the instant a scalding broth is poured over it, so the meat stays pink and tender. Around Yongfu Road and Chihkan Tower there are stalls selling it from early morning — a bowl with a side of minced-pork rice before the temples is the most authentic way to warm up the old-capital way.

food.name: Around Yongfu Road — Traditional Old-Capital Snacks
food.description: The West Central District, where both temples stand, is the densest cluster of Tainan street food in the old city. Savory rice pudding, danzai noodles, shrimp rolls, thin noodles, tofu pudding — every few steps you cross a stall carrying a flavor handed down for decades. After praying to Yue Lao, find a small shop, sit down, and eat slowly, so this solo journey gets a gentle ending.

name: Taipei Yue Lao Love-Praying Escape
transport: By MRT and on foot; an EasyCard is easiest. The two stops are about a 15-minute MRT ride apart.
summary: For praying to Yue Lao in Taipei, the first name that comes to most minds is the Xia-Hai City God Temple in Dadaocheng — but this route sets the order for you. Start the morning at Manka Longshan Temple, letting the stillness of a near-300-year-old temple settle your heart before you ask its Yue Lao, the Matchmaker God, in the rear hall for a good match. Then take the MRT to Dadaocheng and finish at the Xia-Hai City God Temple's Yue Lao — the most trusted and most thronged in all Taiwan. Two stops in half a day, and just right for one person. For quiet, pick a weekday at dawn.

stops.prayFor: A good match, and a settled heart to open the way
stops.why: Longshan Temple is dedicated to Guanyin, the Bodhisattva of Compassion, and its rear hall also houses Yue Lao, the Matchmaker God. Compared with the crowds of Dadaocheng, the Yue Lao here is far quieter — and that is the point of putting it first. In the calm of a near-300-year-old temple, let your heart settle and think through the match you truly want. A settled heart makes a sincere wish.
stops.tips: Longshan Temple no longer burns incense — pressing your palms together to pray is the norm. To pray to Yue Lao, you can bring fresh flowers and wedding candy, and sincerely report your name, birth date, and the match you hope for. The temple is quietest at dawn, and best of all for lingering alone.
stops.arrival: MRT Longshan Temple Station, Exit 1 — about a 2-minute walk

stops.prayFor: A match, a true and lasting love, and a relationship that bears fruit
stops.why: The Yue Lao of the Xia-Hai City God Temple is the most renowned and most incense-heavy Matchmaker God in all Taiwan — travelers fly in from Japan and Korea just to pray here. Its love-praying customs are the most complete anywhere: pray to Yue Lao, take the red thread, offer wedding candy and lead-money coins; and if the match comes good later, remember to return with a box of wedding cookies to thank him. The first stop settled your heart and made the wish; here you hand it to the most trusted Yue Lao to finish.
stops.tips: The temple is small and the worshippers unending; the red thread and offerings can be requested right beside it. Carry the red thread you receive with you, and don't wash it off. To avoid the crowds, be sure to pick a weekday and steer clear of weekends and the run-up to Valentine's Day. After praying, walk down Dihua Street — the century-old dried-goods street is scenery in itself.
stops.arrival: From Longshan Temple Station, take the MRT to Beimen Station (change at Ximen), then Exit 3 and about a 10-minute walk

itinerary.activity: Manka Longshan Temple (Yue Lao — settling the heart and praying for a match)
MRT from Longshan Temple Station to Beimen Station (change at Ximen, about 15 minutes)
Xia-Hai City God Temple (Yue Lao — finishing with the prayer for love)
Lunch on Dihua Street in Dadaocheng, and a slow wander

notes: Both stops are free to enter. This route deliberately saves the most famous — and most crowded — Xia-Hai City God Temple for the finish, so for any quiet at all, be sure to pick a weekday at dawn and avoid weekends, the 1st and 15th of the lunar month, and the run-up to Valentine's Day. There's no rush when you're praying for love — walking alone and thinking things through slowly is meant to be a quiet stretch of time for yourself. If you still have energy that day, Dadaocheng's dried-goods shops and the temple-courtyard food street by Cisheng Temple make a fine extension; if you're spent, save it for next time.

food.name: Manka — Huaxi Street Old-Taipei Eats
food.description: Step out of Longshan Temple and you're in the oldest quarter of Manka, right beside Huaxi Street Night Market. Sesame-oil pork kidney, oyster vermicelli, old-fashioned sweet soups — much of it from shops that have kept the same flavors for decades. A bowl here after praying for love is a taste of a century of Wanhua street life.

food.name: Dadaocheng — Cisheng Temple Courtyard & Dihua Street
food.description: In Dadaocheng, home to the Xia-Hai City God Temple, beyond the dried goods and traditional pastries of Dihua Street, those in the know turn into the food street in front of Cisheng Temple — a long row of tables and chairs under an old banyan tree, with fish soup, fried snacks, and pork-rib soup over rice. It is one of the few places left in Taipei where you can eat quietly in a temple courtyard's shade, and it suits a solo traveler well.

name: Taipei Wenchang Exam-Luck Escape
transport: By MRT and on foot; an EasyCard is easiest. The two stops are about a 5-minute MRT ride apart.
summary: When a big exam is closing in and the nerves start to bite, this is the trip Taipei people make. Start the morning at the Taipei Confucius Temple, asking Confucius — the Great Sage and First Teacher — for a grounded, steady mind for study; then take the MRT to the Taipei Wenchang Temple near Shuanglian to pray to Wenchang Dijun, the god of examinations and literary success, for exam luck and a place on the pass list. One stop for the roots of learning, one stop for the luck to pass — two stops in half a day, enough to settle your own heart, or the heart of a student at home.

stops.prayFor: A foundation in study, an upright approach to learning, and a calm, focused mind
stops.why: The Taipei Confucius Temple is the most important Confucian temple in northern Taiwan. Its Dacheng Hall holds no idols — Confucius, the Great Sage and First Teacher, is honored by a spirit tablet alone, solemn and plain. What you come here to pray for is not last-minute exam luck but a grounded attitude toward study and a settled mind: quiet the heart first, and the reading goes in. That is exactly why this route puts it first.
stops.tips: The Confucius Temple burns no incense — a bow with palms pressed together is all that is needed. The grounds are peaceful, well suited to a slow solo loop to clear your head. The grandest day is the Confucius ceremony (the Shidian rite) on Teachers' Day, September 28, each year; on ordinary days it is far quieter.
stops.arrival: MRT Yuanshan Station, Exit 2 — about a 10-minute walk

stops.prayFor: Exam luck, a place on the pass list, and Wenchang's blessing
stops.why: The Taipei Wenchang Temple stands right by Shuanglian MRT Station and is the busiest Wenchang temple in central Taipei, dedicated to Wenchang Dijun, the god who governs scholarly honors. Come exam season, its walls fill with photocopied exam admission tickets, layer upon layer packed edge to edge — the hopes of countless students, each pinned here for a place on the pass list. Having prayed for the roots of learning, at this stop you hand the luck of passing to Wenchang Dijun.
stops.tips: Tradition calls for 'homophone offerings': scallion (cong, for cleverness), celery (qin, for diligence), radish or caitou (for good fortune), and zongzi rice dumplings (bao-zhong, a 'guaranteed pass'). You can bring a photocopy of the exam admission ticket for Wenchang Dijun to 'register.' Report the student's name, ticket number, and exam subjects sincerely.
stops.arrival: From Yuanshan Station, take the MRT to Shuanglian Station (2 stops), then about a 5-minute walk

itinerary.activity: Taipei Confucius Temple (the Great Sage — praying for a foundation in study and a calm mind)
MRT from Yuanshan Station to Shuanglian Station (about 5 minutes)
Taipei Wenchang Temple (Wenchang Dijun — praying for exam luck and a place on the pass list)
Lunch and a slow wander around Shuanglian and Chifeng Street

notes: Both stops are free to enter. Praying for exam luck isn't praying for a lucky break — this route deliberately places the Confucius Temple's 'foundation for study' ahead of the Wenchang Temple's 'exam-luck blessing,' a reminder to yourself (or the student at home) that a settled heart and diligent reading are what give a god's blessing something to work on. For quiet, pick a weekday morning and avoid the crush in the week before major exams, as well as the 1st and 15th of the lunar month. Afterward, the Shuanglian and Chifeng Street area is full of old shops and cafés — a good place to sit down alone and catch your breath.

food.name: Shuanglian & Chifeng Street — Old-Taipei Flavors
food.description: The Shuanglian and Chifeng Street area around the Wenchang Temple is where old Taipei and the new creative crowd overlap. There's the traditional street food of Shuanglian Morning Market and the old noodle shops and cafés tucked down Chifeng Street's lanes — after praying for exam luck, find a small shop here, have a bowl of noodles or a cup of tea, and let some of the tension ease off.

food.name: Dalongdong — Temple-Gate & Old-Street Eats
food.description: Dalongdong, beside the Confucius Temple, is one of old Taipei's original settlements, right next to Bao'an Temple and Hami Street. The temple-gate snacks and traditional noodle dishes around here are local flavors from shops decades old — after praying at the Confucius Temple in the morning, stop for a late breakfast on the old street before moving on to the next stop.

name: Taipei Evil-Warding & Villain-Dispelling Escape
transport: By MRT and on foot; an EasyCard is easiest. Both stops sit on the same Zhonghe–Xinlu Line, about a 12-minute ride apart.
summary: When petty people are dogging your steps, nothing seems to go right, and there's a knot of grievance sitting in your chest, this is the quiet reset of a trip to take. Start at the Xinzhuang Dizang Temple, where the Civil and Martial Great Sacred Lords — served by the Guanjiangshou spirit-general troupe that was born here — specialize in warding off evil and clearing away the bad energy and the backstabbers clinging to you. Then take the MRT to the Xia-Hai City God Temple in Dadaocheng, where the City God weighs right and wrong and sets things straight. Two stops in half a day: clear out the ill feeling you've been carrying, and walk it alone at an unhurried pace — that is exactly enough.

stops.prayFor: Warding off evil, dispelling petty people, and cutting loose old entanglements
stops.why: The fierce-faced Guanjiangshou (spirit-general troupe) you see at Taiwanese temple processions was born right here, at the Xinzhuang Dizang Temple. Commonly called the 'Great Sacred Temple,' it is dedicated to Dizang (Ksitigarbha) and the Civil and Martial Great Sacred Lords (Wenwu Dazhongye), and it specializes in warding off evil, handling lawsuits, and finding lost things — the most important center of exorcism belief in northern Taiwan. If there are backstabbers, legal troubles, or a run of bad luck you can't shake, coming here to ask the Great Sacred Lords and the Guanjiangshou for a 'clearing out' is the first step this route sets for you.
stops.tips: The Dizang Temple keeps a steady stream of incense, and the temple provides gold paper and instructions. Praying to ward off evil and dispel petty people has its own way of doing things — if you're unsure, ask a temple volunteer. The Guanjiangshou troupe of the annual 'Xinzhuang Grand Worship' (the Great Sacred Lords' procession, on the 1st of the fifth lunar month) is the most striking, but also the most crowded; for quiet, pick a weekday.
stops.arrival: MRT Xinzhuang Station (Zhonghe–Xinlu Line), Exit 1 — about a 5-minute walk

stops.prayFor: A clear judgment of right and wrong, fair dealing, and peace of mind
stops.why: The Xia-Hai City God Temple is famous for its Yue Lao, but the City God it enshrines has a very different primary role: he governs a district's rewards and punishments and judges right from wrong. When you've been wronged, crossed by petty people, or left with an unsettled heart, you come to report it to the City God — what you're really asking for is the calm of trusting that fairness rests in the god's own reckoning. The first stop warded off the evil and dispelled the villains; here you lay right and wrong before the City God to weigh, so you can let go and move on.
stops.tips: The temple is small and the worshippers unending. When you report to the City God, lay out the wrong and the wish plainly — what you seek is a settled certainty and a sense of release. After praying, the temple offers a cup of peace tea; drink it before you go. Then stroll down Dihua Street — the century-old dried-goods street is the best kind of scenery for winding down.
stops.arrival: From Xinzhuang Station, take the MRT to Daqiaotou Station (Zhonghe–Xinlu Line, about 12 minutes), then about a 12-minute walk

itinerary.activity: Xinzhuang Dizang Temple (the Great Sacred Lords & the Guanjiangshou — warding off evil and dispelling petty people)
MRT from Xinzhuang Station to Daqiaotou Station (about 12 minutes)
Xia-Hai City God Temple (the City God — a clear judgment of right and wrong, and fair dealing)
Stroll Dihua Street in Dadaocheng, and lunch

notes: Both stops are free to enter. Warding off evil and dispelling petty people is a folk tradition for finding peace of mind — the point of this trip isn't to resent anyone, but to clear out the ill feeling and grievance you've been carrying, let it go, and set yourself moving forward again. For quiet, pick a weekday morning and avoid the 1st and 15th of the lunar month and weekends. Afterward, Dadaocheng's dried-goods shops and the temple-courtyard food street by Cisheng Temple make a fine extension; if you're spent, save it for next time.

food.name: Dadaocheng — Cisheng Temple Courtyard & Dihua Street
food.description: In Dadaocheng, home to the Xia-Hai City God Temple, beyond the dried goods and traditional pastries of Dihua Street, those in the know turn into the food street in front of Cisheng Temple — a long row of tables and chairs under an old banyan tree, with fish soup, fried snacks, and pork-rib soup over rice. It is one of the few places left in Taipei where you can eat quietly in a temple courtyard's shade, a fitting spot to sit alone once the ill feeling has been cleared away.

food.name: Xinzhuang — Temple-Street Old Flavors
food.description: Xinzhuang Temple Street (around Xinzhuang Road), where the Dizang Temple stands, is one of the oldest market streets in northern Taiwan. Salted 'guangbing' biscuits, traditional noodle dishes, and old pastry shops here carry flavors from businesses decades old — after praying to the Great Sacred Lords, stop for a bite on the old street before moving on to the next stop.
